blocks.text: If, in the face of these so categorically expressed instructions, I nevertheless refuse to perform the Herostratic deed my friend demands of me, I have the most compelling reasons for doing so.
Some of them cannot be discussed in public. Yet even those I can disclose are, in my opinion, quite sufficient to make my decision understood.

The principal reason: when I changed my profession in 1921, I told my friend that I had made my will, in which I asked him to destroy this and that, look through other things, and so forth. Thereupon Kafka said, showing me the outside of the note written in ink which was subsequently found in his desk: “My will shall be quite simple—the request to you to burn everything.” I also remember quite precisely the answer I gave at the time: “If you should seriously expect such a thing of me, I tell you now that I shall not fulfil your request.” The whole conversation was conducted in that jesting tone customary between us, yet with the hidden earnestness which each of us always assumed in the other. Convinced of the earnestness of my refusal, Franz would have had to appoint another executor if his own instructions had been a matter of absolute and final earnest to him.

I am not grateful to him for having plunged me into this grievous conflict of conscience, which he must have foreseen, for he knew the fanatical reverence I bore his every word, and which, throughout the twenty-two years of our never-clouded friendship, prompted me (among other things) never to throw away even the smallest scrap of paper, a single picture postcard, that came from him. — Yet let this “I am not grateful” not be misunderstood! What does even the most grievous conflict of conscience weigh against the infinite blessing I owe to the friend who was the very backbone of my entire spiritual existence!

Further reasons: Franz himself did not obey the injunction on the pencilled sheet, for he later expressly gave permission for portions of ‘Contemplation’ to be reprinted in a newspaper, and for three further stories to be published, which he himself combined with “A Hunger Artist” and handed over to the publishing house Die Schmiede. Both sets of instructions, moreover, date from a time when my friend’s self-critical tendencies had reached their height. In the last year of his life, however, his whole existence took an unforeseen, new, happy, positive turn which supersedes this self-hatred and nihilism. — My decision to publish the literary remains is, moreover, made easier by the recollection of all the bitter struggles by which I wrested every single publication from Kafka and often enough begged it of him. And yet afterwards he was reconciled to these publications and relatively satisfied. — Finally, with a posthumous publication a number of motives cease to apply, for instance, that publication might disturb further work, that it might summon up the shadows of personally painful periods of life. How closely, for Kafka, the withholding of publication was bound up with the problem of the conduct of his life (a problem which, to our immeasurable sorrow, no longer troubles him) is evident, as from many conversations, from the following letter to me: “… I am not enclosing the novels. Why stir up the old efforts? Merely because I have not yet burnt them? … When I next come, it will hopefully be done. Wherein lies the sense of preserving such works, failures ‘even’ in artistic terms? In the hope that these fragments will piece themselves together into a whole, some court of appeal at whose breast I shall be able to beat when I am in distress. I know that this is impossible, that no help comes from that quarter. What, then, am I to do with these things? Are those things which cannot help me to harm me as well, as, given this knowledge, they must?”
